summary: Specifies Protocol Independent Multicast - Sparse Mode, a multicast routing protocol that can use underlying unicast routing information. It builds unidirectional shared trees rooted at a Rendezvous Point for each group, and optionally shortest-path trees per source. It was standards-track and has been replaced by RFC 7761.

plainLanguage.summary: One sender wants to reach many receivers without sending many copies. PIM-SM sets up branching paths so one copy is made only where paths split.

questions: what is a rendezvous point in multicast
how does pim sm build multicast trees
what is a pim assert message
subtitle: How multicast routers build delivery trees across a wide-area network, using a meeting-point router so senders and receivers can find each other.

tldr.problem: Multicast sends one stream to many receivers, but senders and receivers do not know about each other in advance, and flooding traffic everywhere does not scale across wide-area networks.
tldr.mechanism: Receivers' routers send Join messages toward a Rendezvous Point (RP) to build a shared tree. Senders' routers register traffic to the RP, which can join back toward the source, and receivers' routers may then switch to a shortest-path tree.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4601 moved PIM-SM onto the Standards Track, replacing the Experimental RFC 2362. It has since been obsoleted by RFC 7761.

today: RFC 4601 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 7761, which is now the specification to use for PIM-SM. It was also updated by RFC 5059, RFC 5796 and RFC 6226, and it replaced the Experimental RFC 2362.

sections.title: What PIM-SM Is For
sections.content:
RFC 4601 specifies Protocol Independent Multicast - Sparse Mode (PIM-SM), a protocol for efficiently routing multicast groups that may span wide-area and inter-domain internets. It is called protocol independent because it can use the underlying unicast routing to get reverse-path information for building trees, but does not depend on any particular unicast routing protocol.

PIM-SM version 2 was first specified in RFC 2117 and revised in RFC 2362, both Experimental. This document corrects deficiencies found in that earlier text and brings PIM-SM onto the Standards Track. It specifies the same protocol as RFC 2362 wherever possible, and routers built to this document can interoperate with routers built to RFC 2362.

Key terms: the Rendezvous Point (RP) is a router configured as the root of the non-source-specific tree for a group. The Designated Router (DR) acts for directly connected hosts on a LAN. The MRIB is the multicast routing table, often derived from unicast routing, and is used to decide where Join/Prune messages go.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a rulebook that tells routers how to pass one message to many listeners without sending lots of copies.

sections.title: The Three Phases
sections.content:
The overview describes how PIM-SM works in three phases. All three can happen at once, since senders and receivers come and go at any time.

Phase one: the RP tree. A receiver announces interest, typically using IGMP or MLD. Its DR sends a (*,G) Join hop by hop toward the group's RP. Each router along the way creates tree state for group G. The result is the RP Tree, also called the shared tree. A sender just starts sending. Its DR encapsulates the packets in unicast Register messages to the RP, which unwraps them and forwards them down the shared tree.

Phase two: Register-Stop. Encapsulation is expensive and may take a long detour, so the RP normally sends an (S,G) Join toward the source. When the packets arrive natively, the RP drops the encapsulated copies and sends a Register-Stop to the source's DR.

Phase three: the shortest-path tree. A router on the receiver's LAN, typically the DR, may optionally switch to a source-specific shortest-path tree (SPT) by sending an (S,G) Join toward the source. Once traffic arrives that way, it sends an (S,G,rpt) Prune toward the RP so that it stops getting the copy from the shared tree.
sections.plainLanguage: First everyone meets at a middle spot, the RP. Then the sender builds a direct road to the middle spot. Finally, listeners who live far from the middle can build a shortcut straight to the sender.

sections.title: Hello Messages and Designated Routers
sections.content:
Routers discover each other using Hello messages, which are sent periodically on every PIM-enabled interface, including point-to-point links, to the ALL-PIM-ROUTERS group (224.0.0.13 for IPv4 and ff02::d for IPv6). Some implementations skip point-to-point links; the RFC calls this non-compliant. A neighbor will not accept Join/Prune or Assert messages from a router it has not heard a Hello from, so a router must send a Hello first if it has not yet done so.

Hello messages also carry options. The DR_Priority option lets an administrator prefer a router in the DR election, with a default priority of 1. The Generation_Identifier (GenID) is a random 32-bit value regenerated when PIM forwarding starts or restarts, so neighbors can tell that a router rebooted. The LAN Prune Delay and Address List options are also defined.

On each interface one DR is elected. The router with the numerically larger DR Priority wins, and ties go to the higher IP address. If any neighbor on the interface did not include a DR Priority, the election falls back to the highest IP address alone. DR election must run on all active interfaces.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers wave hello to their neighbors every so often. On each street they vote for one of them as the class monitor, which is the DR, and the highest-ranked one wins.

sections.title: Assert Messages and Rendezvous Point Selection
sections.content:
On a shared LAN, two upstream routers may both have valid forwarding state, so duplicate packets appear. PIM does not prevent this. Instead, routers notice the duplicates and run an election with Assert messages. The winner keeps forwarding onto the LAN and the loser stops. The winner is the router with (S,G) state, or otherwise the one with the best metric to the RP or source. Downstream routers hear the Assert and send later Joins to the winner. Each router's (S,G) Assert state machine has three states: NoInfo, Assert Winner and Assert Loser.

Every router in a PIM domain must map a group to the same RP, or black holes appear where some receivers miss some groups. The RFC does not mandate one mechanism. It lists four: static configuration (which every PIM router MUST support), embedded-RP in IPv6 group addresses, Cisco's Auto-RP, and the Bootstrap Router (BSR) mechanism.

When several mappings cover a group, the router takes the longest matching group range, then the highest priority, and finally applies a hash function over the candidate RPs. The highest hash value wins, with ties going to the highest IP address.
sections.plainLanguage: If two grown-ups both hand out the same snack, the kids notice the double and the grown-ups agree that only one will keep doing it. Everyone also agrees in advance on which spot is the meeting point.

sections.title: Message Types and Source-Specific Multicast
sections.content:
The messages in the protocol are Hello, Register, Register-Stop, Join/Prune and Assert. Hello, Join/Prune and Assert are sent to the link-local ALL-PIM-ROUTERS address, so compliant routers do not forward them. Register and Register-Stop are unicast between a DR and an RP.

Join/Prune messages come in several kinds, named by the state they affect: (*,*,RP), (*,G), (S,G) and (S,G,rpt). The (*,*,RP) form exists mostly for compatibility with earlier revisions and its implementation is optional. The RFC defines state machines for each in Section 4.5.

PIM-SM also supports Source-Specific Multicast (SSM) as a strict subset. In IPv4 the range 232.0.0.0/8 is set aside for SSM, and FF3x::/32 for IPv6. For groups in this range a router MUST NOT send (*,G) or (S,G,rpt) Join/Prune messages or Register messages, and an RP MUST NOT forward Register-encapsulated packets for them. A PIM-SSM-only router can skip the Register machinery, the shared-tree state machines and the bootstrap RP election.
sections.plainLanguage: There are only a few kinds of notes: hello, I want this, I do not want this, and who is in charge here. When a listener already knows exactly who the speaker is, the middle meeting spot can be skipped entirely.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Forged messages are the main concern. A forged Hello can make an unauthorized router become the DR, which may disrupt the ability of local hosts to send and receive multicast traffic. A forged Assert can make the legitimate forwarder stop sending to a LAN. A forged Join/Prune can waste bandwidth. Forged unicast Register or Register-Stop messages can let an attacker inject traffic through the RP or stop a legitimate DR from registering packets.

The recommended defense is the IPsec Authentication Header (AH) in transport mode, with security associations configured by the administrator. The anti-replay option SHOULD be enabled. This document does not define how to establish the associations, so manual configuration is assumed. Without cryptography, a router SHOULD offer a way to limit which neighbors it accepts messages from, and a DR MUST NOT register a packet unless its source address is a legal one for the receiving subnet.

Denial of service remains possible. Sending to many different group addresses causes many Register packets, large numbers of forged Joins consume router resources, and a forged (*,*,RP) Join could pull all of a domain's traffic toward one border router.
sections.plainLanguage: Because routers believe what their neighbors tell them, a liar could send them the wrong way. A secret handshake that proves who is talking helps, but it cannot stop every kind of trouble.

messages.label: (*,G) Join
messages.note: Builds the shared tree hop by hop toward the RP.

messages.label: Register (encapsulated data)
messages.note: The sender's data is unicast to the RP.

messages.label: (S,G) Join toward source
messages.note: The RP asks for native traffic from the source.

messages.label: Register-Stop
messages.note: Sent once native packets arrive, so the DR stops encapsulating.
